title: Subtle early alert sign that runs the risk of premature death … and only notice when you eat
text:
If you can no longer taste that sour sweet or those salty fries, you can have a higher risk of premature death.
A new study that analyzes more than 7,000 Americans over 40 who lost their sense of taste before life had a 47 percent higher risk of dying prematurely than people who retained all their ability to taste.
And the results showed that women were more at risk than men. Women who reported a loss of taste in early or medium life had 56 percent more likely to die early than those who did not report any change.
Among men, those with a change in their liking had a 34 percent higher risk of early death.
While the study did not specify an age considered as a premature death, the average life expectancy in the United States is 77 years.
The researchers found that those who experienced a growing decrease in salty and sour tastes had a higher risk, at approximately 50 percent greater risk in general.
The newspaper said that the loss of flavor itself was not causing death, but it could be a warning sign of a serious underlying condition that could lead to an earlier death.
Previous studies have related a sense of deteriorated flavor, experienced by approximately 20 percent of people 40 years or older, with being an early indicator of Alzheimer’s disease and heat conditions, such as high blood pressure, It is known that they limit life.
The researchers affirm that a person who cannot recognize salinity and acidity, since it goes from early and late adulthood, can have approximately 50 percent possibilities of mortality.

Writing in the document, the researchers said: “These findings suggest that the subjective perception of the loss of flavor can serve as a simple and valuable indicator to evaluate high -risk populations in the clinic and the practice of public health.”
In humans, the sense of taste is one of the five basic senses and allows people to interpret the world around them.
It is controlled by chemical reactions with flavor receptors in the tongue, and also by responses to cell foods in the nose or smell system.
There are five main tastes that humans experience: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and salty.
Factors such as a cold or flu, sinus infections, allergies, head injuries, hormonal changes, smoking and nutritional deficiencies such as zinc and vitamin B12 can affect taste papillae.
Almost one in five, around 19 percent, of Americans over 40 years of age has reported some alteration in their sense of taste.
A historical maximum of 27 percent of people 80 years or more report the most alterations in their sense of taste.
He study Published on Thursday in Jama Otolaryngology -head & Neck Surgery, it focused on 7,340 Americans of 40 years or more.
The participants were tracked for almost a decade and asked about their sense of taste.
The researchers wrote in their article: ‘These findings support the initiative of the United States initiative and the People 2030 sensory initiative, which aims to detect and prevent sensory disorders to improve the quality of life of affected people.
“These findings suggest that the subjective perception of the loss of flavor can serve as a simple and valuable indicator to evaluate high -risk populations in clinical and public health practices.”
The group, which included 662 people with some form of loss of perceived flavor, was monitored for a period of six to seven years.
Over the years, participants were also asked if their smell and ability to try salt, bittersweet, sweetness and bitterness were better, worse or had no changes compared to when they were 25 years in a detailed questionnaire.
In terms of cumulative decline, they were classified into three groups: without decrease in the perception of any basic taste; decrease in the perception of one or two basic tastes and decrease in the perception of three or four basic tastes
During this time, 1,011 people died, indicating that the typical premature death rate was around one in seven people.
In addition, the study revealed that a loss of flavor can also negatively affect eating habits.
Those who cannot try salt can end up encouraging more salty foods and be more susceptible to high blood pressure.
While those with a limited sensation of sweetness can increase the intake of sweets and sugars added, resulting in metabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes.
The researchers also found that there was a higher risk of death in people who lost their sense of taste but were still completely capable of smelling.
